Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
A specific temperature on the skin

Maladaptive Strategies.value: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows
I work hard at keeping busy with other things

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

vignette: Sami, a 48-year-old Middle Eastern man and a fashion designer, has been struggling to cope with the aftermath of a man-made disaster that he experienced several months ago. The event was so traumatic that it left him with fragmented memories that often feel like they are happening all over again. Sami’s daily life is punctuated by sudden intrusive memories that bring back vivid sensory details from the trauma. One such trigger occurred recently while he was at work, feeling a specific temperature on his skin that matched the ambient temperature of the disaster scene. The memory hit him so forcefully that he felt nauseous and had to excuse himself from the bustling design studio where he works. This is when Sami’s maladaptive strategies kicked in; he would often hurt himself physically to release the overwhelming feelings, or work himself into a frenzy by keeping busy with other tasks. The fragmented nature of his memories has made it difficult for him to piece together what happened during the disaster. The memory feels present and not past, and when triggered, it is accompanied by a vivid taste that he associates with the event. This disjointed recollection often leads to an acute sense of danger, which drives Sami’s heightened threat monitoring behaviors. He constantly scans his surroundings for signs of danger and always identifies escape routes before feeling comfortable anywhere. These fragmented memories also lead directly to his maladaptive strategies. When a memory intrudes, he becomes hyper-focused on the details, unable to concentrate on anything else. To cope with this intense focus, Sami resorts to self-harm or busyness to distract himself from the overwhelming sense of danger and discomfort. The trauma has significantly impacted his work environment. His need for constant distraction through busyness means that he often neglects important tasks, leading to increased stress and tension in his professional relationships. Additionally, the repeated checking of locks and windows at home is a clear sign that Sami’s maladaptive strategies are deeply intertwined with his threat perception. Sami’s fear has grown into a self-reinforcing cycle over time. The more he focuses on the fragmented memories and their vivid sensory details, the greater his sense of danger becomes. This heightened state then leads him to engage in even more maladaptive behaviors as coping mechanisms, further exacerbating his condition. He has come to believe that he needs to be constantly vigilant and prepared for any potential threat. What finally brought Sami to seek help was a combination of mounting stress at work and the realization that his self-harm had escalated to a point where it could no longer be ignored. He is most afraid of losing control over these intense feelings, but he also hopes for a way to regain some sense of normalcy in his daily life. Sami’s story illustrates how the traumatic event has led him into a cycle of intrusive memories, heightened threat perceptions, and maladaptive coping strategies that have significantly impacted both his personal and professional life.
